J. L. Austin is called a naive empiricist because his ordinary-language method treats “what we should say when,” collected case by case, as philosophy’s basic evidence. In *A Plea for Excuses*, *Sense and Sensibilia*, and *How to Do Things with Words*, he held that cataloguing those everyday distinctions would dissolve traditional problems. “Naive” marks the assumption that ordinary usage is straightforward, theory-neutral data and that describing it is enough to settle the questions.
